identification.summary: JINX-0164 is a name used by Wiz Research for a financially motivated cluster, disclosed in late May 2026, that targets cryptocurrency organizations and software developers, almost entirely on macOS [S5][S7]. Intrusions start with fake recruiter approaches on LinkedIn that steer victims to a fake video-conferencing page, which delivers the AUDIOFIX Python infostealer/RAT; the actor then moves from developer laptops into code repositories and CI/CD pipelines [S5][S6][S7]. In April 2026 it trojanized version 9.4.1 of the npm package @velora-dex/sdk to deliver the MINIRAT Go backdoor [S5][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Activity dates to at least mid-2025 per Wiz [S5][S7]. Public disclosure: Wiz, late May 2026 [S5][S7].
identification.notes: JINX-0164 is a Wiz-assigned cluster name, not a Microsoft name; no Microsoft actor name or MITRE group was found in the sources gathered. The trojanized npm version is 9.4.1 (published 2026-04-07; clean baseline 9.4.0; reverted in 9.4.2 about three hours later per SafeDep/OpenSourceMalware); one secondary outlet's '4.9.1' is a typo [S6]. Wiz is reported as noting consistency with DPRK financially motivated groups without confirmed overlap or formal attribution (see attribution).

attribution.confidence: Wiz tracks the cluster as financially motivated and, as reported by secondary outlets, has not formally attributed it to a state actor, though it notes consistency with DPRK financially motivated groups [S5][S7]. This record's imported country field (KP) is not supported by a primary source gathered here.
attribution.basis: Per secondary coverage, Wiz assesses the activity as consistent with North Korean financially motivated groups (BlueNoroff, Contagious Interview, UNC1069/Sapphire Sleet) but with distinct infrastructure and no confirmed overlap; it has not formally attributed the cluster to DPRK [S5][S7]. A Cloud Security Alliance research note is reported as saying the actor does not appear to operate at the scale of large North Korea-linked crypto thefts while using similar foundational techniques [S3]. These are technique-level similarities, not attribution.

objectives: Financial gain: theft of cryptocurrency and wallet credentials from developers, plus access to code and CI/CD systems at crypto firms for follow-on compromise [S5][S7].

targeting.notes: Targeting is by role and sector (macOS-using developers at crypto organizations) rather than by geography; regions not stated in the sources gathered [S5][S7].

capabilities.summary: Credible LinkedIn recruiter personas and fake meeting pages spoofing Teams-style conferencing; a shell script that profiles the system and fetches payloads from a fake driver-store domain; AUDIOFIX (Python macOS infostealer/RAT) and MINIRAT (lightweight Go backdoor sharing C2 with AUDIOFIX) [S5][S6][S7]. After initial access the actor injected AUDIOFIX into internal repositories with commits disguised under other developers' names, so colleagues building from them were infected [S5]. It also compromised an npm publisher account (not the GitHub source) to push a trojanized package [S6]. Secondary coverage says AUDIOFIX targets 51 cryptocurrency wallet browser extensions [S7].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Developer workstations (macOS), source repositories, package registry accounts and CI/CD runners are key terrain; for DoD this maps to software factories and contractor developers, though sources show only crypto-sector targeting. STEP 2: The actor exploits trust in recruiters, meeting links and upstream packages rather than software vulnerabilities [S5][S6]. STEP 3: Template: LinkedIn lure, fake meeting page, shell script, AUDIOFIX, repository/commit tampering, CI/CD access, package publishing [S5][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued crypto-developer targeting for theft. MDCOA is the same tradecraft aimed at defense software developers or widely used packages to seed supply-chain access; this is analyst projection, not sourced. Candidate indicators: unexpected npm releases without matching git tags, commits under a developer's name from unusual hosts, outbound traffic to datahub[.]ink, cloud-sync[.]online, byte-io[.]us [S5][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track package-integrity and registry-account alerts for mission software. (2) Authorities: developer endpoints and CI/CD often sit with contractors or program offices; clarify who may isolate or investigate. (3) Mission assurance: protect signing keys, publish tokens and pipeline secrets; require artifact-to-source verification. (4) Coordination: share IOCs through DC3/DIB channels; treat attribution to state actors as unconfirmed [S3][S5].

provenance.importedSummary: JINX-0164 is a financially motivated threat actor active since mid-2025, primarily targeting software developers through recruitment-themed social engineering to steal cryptocurrencies and conduct supply chain attacks. Their operations have focused on macOS devices, utilizing malware such as AUDIOFIX and MINIRAT, with a notable supply chain compromise involving the trojanization of an npm package. The actor employs a shell script for initial system profiling and payload delivery, often spoofing legitimate services like Microsoft Teams and cryptocurrency companies. JINX-0164's infrastructure includes numerous lookalike domains and utilizes VPN exit nodes for accessing victim systems.
